# Implication

## Implication {.smaller}

Connect operator $\rightarrow$ to a logically equivalent expression using only *and*, *or*, and *not*.

| $p$ | $q$ | $p\rightarrow q$ | $\underline{\hspace{3em}}$ |
|-----|-----|:----------------:|:--------------------------:|
| F   | F   |        T         |                            |
| F   | T   |        T         |                            |
| T   | F   |        F         |                            |
| T   | T   |        T         |                            |

-   Note: $p \rightarrow q \equiv$ \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

-   $p \rightarrow q$ Corresponds to "if $p$ then $q$"

-   We’re not promising causation, only a truth condition.

-   $p \rightarrow q$ is `False` **only** when $p$ is `True` and $q$ is `False`.

-   Gives us mechanism for reasoning!

-   Is this operator commutative?

## Converses — check what’s `True` {.activity .smaller}

Each of the following is $p\rightarrow q$. &emsp; Underline $p$, [dash-underline]{.dashed} $q$. &emsp; Then decide whether each direction is true.

| # | Statement | p→q | q→p |
|:-:|---|:--:|:--:|
| 1 | If it’s a kitten, then it’s a cat. | ☐ | ☐ |
| 2 | If an animal is a mammal, then it is a cat. | ☐ | ☐ |
| 3 | If I’m an only child, then I have zero siblings. | ☐ | ☐ |
| 4 | If I eat breakfast, then I ace the quiz. | ☐ | ☐ |
| 5 | A player is in the NHL only if they are a professional. | ☐ | ☐ |
| 6 | To be empty, a string must have length 0. | ☐ | ☐ |
| 7 | No song appears on the Billboard Hot 100 without reaching #1. | ☐ | ☐ |
: {tbl-colwidths="[5,81,7,7]"}

{{< countdown minutes=8 >}}

::: notes
Two steps per row, and only the first is logic:

  TRANSLATE -- what does the sentence assert?   EVALUATE -- is that true?

Rows 1-4 translate for free ("if" names the antecedent). Rows 5-7 do not:

  5  "only if" marks the CONSEQUENT. Students read "p only if q" as q->p
     because "if" sits next to q. It means p->q.
  6  "must" -- necessity, so again the consequent.
  7  Board work. THE HARD PART IS FINDING p AND q, not the algebra below.

     The sentence carries two negation words -- "No" and "without" -- and
     NEITHER belongs to p or q. Both are structural. p and q are positive:

       p: this song appears on the Hot 100
       q: this song reached #1

     Ask "what two facts about a single song does this sentence relate?"
     That strips the scaffolding and leaves the atoms. Each is plainly
     true-or-false of one song; neither contains a "no" or a "without".
     Students will want q = "does not reach #1", or will attach the "No"
     to p. Underline only the positive spans.

     Once p and q are fixed, *without* = *and not* and the rest is algebra:

       ~(p ^ ~q)  ==  ~p v ~~q     De Morgan        (lecture 3 laws table)
                  ==  ~p v q       double negation  (same table)
                  ==  p -> q       definition of -> (slide 1 today)

     This is the first CHAIN OF EQUIVALENCES in the course -- lecture 3
     promised two ways to justify an equivalence, and only truth tables have
     been used so far. It is also the worked example for the LE Proof slide
     two slides from now.

     Then the catch: the chain shows the sentence MEANS p->q. It does not
     show p->q is true -- and it isn't. A song that charted but never hit #1
     makes p true, q false, which falsifies BOTH forms. That is what the
     equivalence promised.

     But the CONVERSE is true, and for a different kind of reason:
       p->q  (charted -> hit #1)   FALSE, empirically -- most never do.
       q->p  (hit #1 -> charted)   TRUE, definitionally -- #1 IS a position
                                   on the Hot 100. You cannot top a chart
                                   you are not on.
     So the sentence asserts the contingent direction, which fails, while the
     direction it does not assert holds by definition. Not a biconditional.

     Same truth pattern as row 2 (mammal -> cat), which they met early and
     easily. Row 7 is that pattern in disguise -- worth pointing back to it.

Row 4 (breakfast/quiz) is the discussion row, not a quick one. Nobody in the
room has the facts, so ask what would make it FALSE -- one day you ate
breakfast and did not ace. That is a counterexample, three lectures early.
It is also the only home for vacuous truth: if you never eat breakfast, p is
always false and the statement is true, because you never broke the promise.

Rows 3 and 4 are the only propositional ones -- about a fixed "I". The rest
range over a domain, which is what predicates are for. Do not say "for all"
yet; it becomes the callback when quantifiers arrive.
:::


## Vocabulary {.smaller}

Given $p\rightarrow q$, we define the following 3 terms:

* \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ is $\neg q\rightarrow \neg p$

* \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ is $q\rightarrow p$

* \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ is $\neg p\rightarrow \neg q$

## Biconditionals

We have a special operator for those implications whose converses are 
also `True`:

|   $(p\rightarrow q) \wedge (q\rightarrow p)\equiv p\leftrightarrow q$

Some phrases describing this relationship:

* biconditional
* if and only if (iff)
* equivalent

Which of the seven statements were biconditionals?
